claims.text: Enhanced interfacial lattice distortion governs resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings.
Interfacial lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion reduces creep relative to monolithic coatings.
The proposed multilayers have well-defined, chemically distinct interfaces.
The multilayers exhibit significant lattice distortion owing to random atomic mixing.
Creep deformation is active at approximately 0.4–0.6 times the alloy melting temperature.
A controlled inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation during the creep test.
Engineered interfaces introduce high lattice strain.
Interfacial lattice strain and misfit-dislocation structures act as barriers to dislocation glide and climb.
Under high temperature and constant stress, interfacial lattice distortions create energy barriers that restrict dislocation movement across multilayer boundaries.
Interfacial pinning reduces the accumulation of creep strain compared with single-phase monolithic coatings.
Multilayer coatings will exhibit significantly lower creep rates than monolithic high-entropy-alloy coatings under identical test conditions.
The relevant baseline is a single-phase monolithic high-entropy-alloy coating with the same overall composition but without the interface-engineered multilayer structure.
The proposed mechanism applies only when temperature is high enough to activate creep but low enough to avoid interface degradation or oxidation.
Diffusion-induced coarsening can degrade the multilayer interfaces.
Outside the stated temperature and environmental range, mechanisms other than interface pinning may dominate creep behavior.
Layer thickness and interface sharpness may modulate the proposed pinning effect.
